verses.zh: 众税吏和罪人都挨近耶稣，要听他讲道。
verses.en: Now all the tax collectors[NOTE:1] and sinners were coming[NOTE:2] to hear him.
notes: See the note on tax collectors in 3:12.
Grk “were drawing near.”

verses.zh: 法利赛人和文士私下议论说：「这个人接待罪人，又同他们吃饭。」
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] the Pharisees[NOTE:2] and the experts in the law[NOTE:3] were complaining,[NOTE:4] “This man welcomes[NOTE:5] sinners and eats with them.”
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context.
See the note on Pharisees in 5:17.
Or “and the scribes.” See the note on the phrase “experts in the law” in 5:21.
Or “grumbling”; Grk “were complaining, saying.” The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Or “accepts,” “receives.” This is not the first time this issue has been raised: Luke 5:27-32; 7:37-50.

verses.zh: 耶稣就用比喻说：
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] Jesus[NOTE:2] told them[NOTE:3] this parable:[NOTE:4]
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate that Jesus’ telling of the parable is in response to the complaints of the Pharisees and experts in the law.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Them means at the minimum the parable is for the leadership, but probably also for those people Jesus accepted, but the leaders regarded as outcasts.
Grk “parable, saying.” The participle λέγων (legōn) is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

verses.zh: 「你们中间谁有一百只羊失去一只，不把这九十九只撇在旷野、去找那失去的羊，直到找着呢？
verses.en: “Which one[NOTE:1] of you, if he has a hundred[NOTE:2] sheep and loses one of them, would not leave the ninety-nine in the open pasture[NOTE:3] and go look for[NOTE:4] the one that is lost until he finds it?[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “What man.” The Greek word ἄνθρωπος (anthrōpos) is used here in a somewhat generic sense.
This individual with a hundred sheep is a shepherd of modest means, as flocks often had up to two hundred head of sheep.
Or “desert,” but here such a translation might suggest neglect of the 99 sheep left behind.
Grk “go after,” but in contemporary English the idiom “to look for” is used to express this.
Until he finds it. The parable pictures God’s pursuit of the sinner. On the image of Jesus as the Good Shepherd, see John 10:1-18.

verses.zh: 找着了，就欢欢喜喜地扛在肩上，回到家里，
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] when he has found it, he places it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.

verses.zh: 就请朋友邻舍来，对他们说：『我失去的羊已经找着了，你们和我一同欢喜吧！』
verses.en: Returning[NOTE:1] home, he calls together[NOTE:2] his[NOTE:3] friends and neighbors, telling them, ‘Rejoice with me because I have found my sheep that was lost.’
notes: Grk “And coming into his…” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
A touch of drama may be present, as the term calls together can mean a formal celebration (1 Kgs 1:9-10).

Grk “the”; in context the article is used as a possessive pronoun (ExSyn 215). It occurs before “neighbors” as well (“his friends and his neighbors”) but has not been translated the second time because of English style.

verses.zh: 我告诉你们，一个罪人悔改，在天上也要这样为他欢喜，较比为九十九个不用悔改的义人欢喜更大。」
verses.en: I tell you, in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner[NOTE:1] who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people[NOTE:2] who have no need to repent.[NOTE:3]
notes: There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. The pursuit of the sinner is a priority in spite of the presence of others who are doing well (see also Luke 5:32; 19:10). The theme of repentance, a major Lukan theme, is again emphasized.
Here δικαίοις (dikaiois) is an adjective functioning substantivally and has been translated “righteous people.”
Or “who do not need to repent”; Grk “who do not have need of repentance.”

verses.zh: 「或是一个妇人有十块钱，若失落一块，岂不点上灯，打扫屋子，细细地找，直到找着吗？
verses.en: “Or what woman, if she has ten silver coins[NOTE:1] and loses[NOTE:2] one of them,[NOTE:3] does not light a lamp, sweep[NOTE:4] the house, and search thoroughly until she finds it?
notes: This silver coin is a drachma, equal to a denarius, that is, a day’s pay for the average laborer.

Grk “What woman who has ten silver coins, if she loses.” The initial participle ἔχουσα (echousa) has been translated as a finite verb parallel to ἀπολέσῃ (apolesē) in the conditional clause to improve the English style.
Grk “one coin.”
Grk “and sweep,” but καί (kai) has not been translated since English normally uses a coordinating conjunction only between the last two elements in a series of three or more.

verses.zh: 找着了，就请朋友邻舍来，对他们说：『我失落的那块钱已经找着了，你们和我一同欢喜吧！』
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] when she has found it, she calls together her[NOTE:2] friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice[NOTE:3] with me, for I have found the coin[NOTE:4] that I had lost.’
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “the”; in context the article is used as a possessive pronoun (ExSyn 215).
Rejoice. Besides the theme of pursuing the lost, the other theme of the parable is the joy of finding them.
Grk “drachma.”

verses.zh: 我告诉你们，一个罪人悔改，在　神的使者面前也是这样为他欢喜。」
verses.en: In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels[NOTE:1] over one sinner who repents.”
notes: The whole of heaven is said to rejoice. Joy in the presence of God’s angels is a way of referring to God’s joy as well without having to name him explicitly. Contemporary Judaism tended to refer to God indirectly where possible out of reverence or respect for the divine name.

verses.zh: 耶稣又说：「一个人有两个儿子。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Jesus[NOTE:2] said, “A man had two sons.
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 小儿子对父亲说：『父亲，请你把我应得的家业分给我。』他父亲就把产业分给他们。
verses.en: The[NOTE:1] younger of them said to his[NOTE:2] father, ‘Father, give me the share of the estate[NOTE:3] that will belong[NOTE:4] to me.’ So[NOTE:5] he divided his[NOTE:6] assets between them.[NOTE:7]
notes: Grk “And the.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “the”; in context the article is used as a possessive pronoun (ExSyn 215).
L&N 57.19 notes that in nonbiblical contexts in which the word οὐσία (ousia) occurs, it refers to considerable possessions or wealth, thus “estate.”
L&N 57.3, “to belong to or come to belong to, with the possible implication of by right or by inheritance.”
Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the father’s response to the younger son’s request.
Grk “the”; in context the article is used as a possessive pronoun (ExSyn 215).
He divided his assets between them. There was advice against doing this in the OT Apocrypha (Sir 33:20). The younger son would get half of what the older son received (Deut 21:17).

verses.zh: 过了不多几日，小儿子就把他一切所有的都收拾起来，往远方去了。在那里任意放荡，浪费资财。
verses.en: After[NOTE:1] a few days,[NOTE:2] the younger son gathered together all he had and left on a journey to a distant country, and there he squandered[NOTE:3] his wealth[NOTE:4] with a wild lifestyle.
notes: Grk “And after.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “after not many days.”
Or “wasted.” This verb is graphic; it means to scatter (L&N 57.151).
Or “estate” (the same word has been translated “estate” in v. 12).

verses.zh: 既耗尽了一切所有的，又遇着那地方大遭饥荒，就穷苦起来。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] after he had spent everything, a severe famine took place in that country, and he began to be in need.
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the sequence of events in the parable. Greek style often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” but English style generally does not.

verses.zh: 于是去投靠那地方的一个人；那人打发他到田里去放猪。
verses.en: So he went and worked for[NOTE:1] one of the citizens of that country, who[NOTE:2] sent him to his fields to feed pigs.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “joined himself to” (in this case an idiom for beginning to work for someone).
Grk “and he.” Here the conjunction καί (kai) and the personal pronoun have been translated by a relative pronoun to improve the English style.
To a Jew, being sent to the field to feed pigs would be an insult, since pigs were considered unclean animals (Lev 11:7).

verses.zh: 他恨不得拿猪所吃的豆荚充饥，也没有人给他。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] was longing to eat[NOTE:2] the carob pods[NOTE:3] the pigs were eating, but[NOTE:4] no one gave him anything.
notes: Grk “And he.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Or “would gladly have eaten”; Grk “was longing to be filled with.”

This term refers to the edible pods from a carob tree (BDAG 540 s.v. κεράτιον). They were bean-like in nature and were commonly used for fattening pigs, although they were also used for food by poor people (L&N 3.46).
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context.

verses.zh: 他醒悟过来，就说：『我父亲有多少的雇工，口粮有余，我倒在这里饿死吗？
verses.en: But when he came to his senses,[NOTE:1] he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired workers have food[NOTE:2] enough to spare, but here I am dying from hunger!
notes: Grk “came to himself” (an idiom).
Grk “bread,” but used figuratively for food of any kind (L&N 5.1).

verses.zh: 我要起来，到我父亲那里去，向他说：父亲！我得罪了天，又得罪了你；
verses.en: I will get up and go to my father and say to him, “Father, I have sinned[NOTE:1] against heaven[NOTE:2] and against[NOTE:3] you.
notes: In the confession “I have sinned” there is a recognition of wrong that pictures the penitent coming home and “being found.”
The phrase against heaven is a circumlocution for God.
According to BDAG 342 s.v. ἐνωπιον 4.a, “in relation to ἁμαρτάνειν ἐ. τινος sin against someone Lk 15:18, 21 (cp. Jdth 5:17; 1 Km 7:6; 20:1).”

verses.zh: 从今以后，我不配称为你的儿子，把我当作一个雇工吧！』
verses.en: I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me[NOTE:1] like one of your hired workers.”’
notes: Or “make me.” Here is a sign of total humility.

verses.zh: 于是起来，往他父亲那里去。相离还远，他父亲看见，就动了慈心，跑去抱着他的颈项，连连与他亲嘴。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he got up and went to his father. But while he was still a long way from home[NOTE:2] his father saw him, and his heart went out to him;[NOTE:3] he ran and hugged[NOTE:4] his son[NOTE:5] and kissed him.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the result of the son’s decision to return home. Greek style often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” but English style generally does not.
Grk “a long way off from [home].” The word “home” is implied (L&N 85.16).

Or “felt great affection for him,” “felt great pity for him.”sn The major figure of the parable, the forgiving father, represents God the Father and his compassionate response. God is ready with open arms to welcome the sinner who comes back to him.
Grk “he fell on his neck,” an idiom for showing special affection for someone by throwing one’s arms around them. The picture is of the father hanging on the son’s neck in welcome.
Grk “him”; the referent (the son) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 儿子说：『父亲！我得罪了天，又得罪了你；从今以后，我不配称为你的儿子。』
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] his son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven[NOTE:2] and against you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’[NOTE:3]
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
The phrase against heaven is a circumlocution for God. 1st century Judaism tended to minimize use of the divine name out of reverence.
The younger son launches into his confession just as he had planned. See vv. 18-19.

verses.zh: 父亲却吩咐仆人说：『把那上好的袍子快拿出来给他穿；把戒指戴在他指头上；把鞋穿在他脚上；
verses.en: But the father said to his slaves,[NOTE:1] ‘Hurry! Bring the best robe,[NOTE:2] and put it on him! Put a ring on his finger[NOTE:3] and sandals[NOTE:4] on his feet!
notes: See the note on the word “slave” in 7:2.
With the instructions Hurry! Bring the best robe, there is a total acceptance of the younger son back into the home.
Grk “hand,” but χείρ (cheir) can refer to either the whole hand or any relevant part of it (L&N 8.30).
The need for sandals underlines the younger son’s previous destitution because he was barefoot.

verses.zh: 把那肥牛犊牵来宰了，我们可以吃喝快乐；
verses.en: Bring[NOTE:1] the fattened calf[NOTE:2] and kill it! Let us eat[NOTE:3] and celebrate,
notes: Grk “And bring.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style. Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation.
Or “the prize calf” (L&N 65.8). See also L&N 44.2, “grain-fattened.” Such a calf was usually reserved for religious celebrations.
The participle φαγόντες (phagontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 因为我这个儿子是死而复活，失而又得的。』他们就快乐起来。
verses.en: because this son of mine was dead, and is alive again—he was lost and is found!’[NOTE:1] So[NOTE:2] they began to celebrate.
notes: This statement links the parable to the theme of 15:6, 9.
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the result of the father’s remarks in the preceding verses.

verses.zh: 那时，大儿子正在田里。他回来，离家不远，听见作乐跳舞的声音，
verses.en: “Now his older son was in the field. As[NOTE:1] he came and approached the house, he heard music[NOTE:2] and dancing.
notes: Grk “And as.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
This would have been primarily instrumental music, but might include singing as well.

verses.zh: 便叫过一个仆人来，问是甚么事。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he called one of the slaves[NOTE:2] and asked what was happening.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the result of the older son hearing the noise of the celebration in progress.
The Greek term here, παῖς (pais), describes a slave, possibly a household servant regarded with some affection (L&N 87.77).

verses.zh: 仆人说：『你兄弟来了；你父亲因为得他无灾无病地回来，把肥牛犊宰了。』
verses.en: The slave replied,[NOTE:1] ‘Your brother has returned, and your father has killed the fattened calf[NOTE:2] because he got his son[NOTE:3] back safe and sound.’
notes: Grk “And he said to him.” Here δέ (de) has not been translated. The rest of the phrase has been simplified to “the slave replied,” with the referent (the slave) specified in the translation for clarity.
See note on the phrase “fattened calf” in v. 23.
Grk “him”; the referent (the younger son) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 大儿子却生气，不肯进去；他父亲就出来劝他。
verses.en: But the older son[NOTE:1] became angry[NOTE:2] and refused[NOTE:3] to go in. His father came out and appealed to him,
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (the older son, v. 25) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The aorist verb ὠργίσθη (ōrgisthē) has been translated as an ingressive aorist, reflecting entry into a state or condition.
Ironically the attitude of the older son has left him outside and without joy.

verses.zh: 他对父亲说：『我服事你这多年，从来没有违背过你的命，你并没有给我一只山羊羔，叫我和朋友一同快乐。
verses.en: but he answered[NOTE:1] his father, ‘Look! These many years I have worked like a slave[NOTE:2] for you, and I never disobeyed your commands. Yet[NOTE:3] you never gave me even a goat[NOTE:4] so that I could celebrate with my friends!
notes: Grk “but answering, he said.” This is somewhat redundant in contemporary English and has been simplified to “but he answered.”
Or simply, “have served,” but in the emotional context of the older son’s outburst the translation given is closer to the point.
Here καί (kai) has been translated as “yet” to bring out the contrast indicated by the context.
You never gave me even a goat. The older son’s complaint was that the generous treatment of the younger son was not fair: “I can’t get even a little celebration with a basic food staple like a goat!”

verses.zh: 但你这个儿子和娼妓吞尽了你的产业，他一来了，你倒为他宰了肥牛犊。』
verses.en: But when this son of yours[NOTE:1] came back, who has devoured[NOTE:2] your assets with prostitutes,[NOTE:3] you killed the fattened calf[NOTE:4] for him!’
notes: Note the younger son is not “my brother” but this son of yours (an expression with a distinctly pejorative nuance).
This is another graphic description. The younger son’s consumption had been like a glutton. He had both figuratively and literally devoured the assets which were given to him.
The charge concerning the prostitutes is unproven, but essentially the older brother accuses the father of committing an injustice by rewarding his younger son’s unrighteous behavior.
See note on the phrase “fattened calf” in v. 23.

verses.zh: 父亲对他说：『儿啊！你常和我同在，我一切所有的都是你的；
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] the father[NOTE:2] said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and everything that belongs to me is yours.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events in the parable.
Grk “he”; the referent (the father) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 只是你这个兄弟是死而复活、失而又得的，所以我们理当欢喜快乐。』」
verses.en: It was appropriate[NOTE:1] to celebrate and be glad, for your brother[NOTE:2] was dead, and is alive; he was lost and is found.’”[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “necessary.”
By referring to him as your brother, the father reminded the older brother that the younger brother was part of the family.

The theme he was lost and is found is repeated from v. 24. The conclusion is open-ended. The reader is left to ponder with the older son (who pictures the scribes and Pharisees) what the response will be. The parable does not reveal the ultimate response of the older brother. Jesus argued that sinners should be pursued and received back warmly when they returned.
